executive_summary: Analysis terminated early: Pipeline exceeded 1800s wall-clock limit. Partial results below.

findings.clause_text: Within [***] after the end of each Calendar Quarter during the Term, Dova shall provide to Valeant a written report setting forth in reasonable detail the calculation of the Net Sales for such Calendar Quarter and the promotion fee payable in respect of such Net Sales in accordance with Section 6.1
findings.description: Undefined reporting timeline creates uncertainty for Valeant's cash flow planning and enforcement rights
findings.reasoning: The reporting deadline is redacted as [***], leaving Valeant without certainty as to when it will receive the quarterly reports necessary to verify its promotion fee calculations. This creates operational risk for the promoter who needs timely data to manage its business and potentially dispute calculations. The redacted nature suggests this was negotiated but the blank creates ambiguity in enforcement.
findings.remediation: Negotiate to specify a concrete number of days (e.g., 30 or 45 days) for the reporting deadline, or at minimum establish that the reporting deadline must be no later than the payment deadline of 60 days to ensure Valeant has adequate time to review before payment is due.

findings.clause_text: Within sixty (60) days after the end of each Calendar Quarter during the Term, Dova shall pay to Valeant the undisputed portion of the promotion fee payable in respect of such Net Sales in accordance with Section 6.1
findings.description: Payment obligation limited to 'undisputed portion' without defined dispute resolution timeline or escrow mechanism
findings.reasoning: Dova can withhold payment indefinitely by claiming any portion is 'disputed' without any contractual obligation to specify disputes promptly, place disputed funds in escrow, or resolve disputes within a defined timeframe. This creates significant cash flow risk for Valeant as promoter and could lead to prolonged payment delays. The 60-day payment window for undisputed amounts is reasonable, but the lack of constraints on the disputed portion mechanism undermines it.
findings.remediation: Add requirements that: (a) Dova must specify any disputed items within [X] days of report receipt; (b) disputed amounts must be placed in escrow or subject to expedited resolution; (c) undisputed amounts must be paid within 60 days regardless of other disputes; (d) disputes resolved in Valeant's favor bear interest from original due date.

findings.clause_text: If this Agreement terminates or expires during a Calendar Quarter, the promotion fee payable to Valeant under Section 6.1 will be calculated only on the Net Sales that occurred during such Calendar Quarter prior to the effective date of such termination or expiration
findings.description: No pro-rata payment for post-termination sales attributable to Valeant's pre-termination promotion activities
findings.reasoning: The clause cuts off Valeant's entitlement at the termination date without considering the carryover effect of its promotional activities. Pharmaceutical sales often have significant lag between promotion and prescription fulfillment; Valeant's pre-termination detailing may generate sales post-termination for which it receives no compensation. This is a standard tension in co-promotion agreements but the provision appears one-sided without any wind-down or trailing commission period.
findings.remediation: Negotiate a trailing commission period (e.g., 90-180 days) for sales of Product shipped to patients based on prescriptions written during the Term, or based on prescriptions from physicians detailed by Valeant during the Term, to capture the lag effect of promotional activities.

findings.clause_text: such examination shall not take place more often than once per every twelve (12) months during the Term and once during the one (1) year period following the end of the Term
findings.description: Asymmetric audit rights - Valeant has no corresponding audit rights against Dova despite Dova controlling all revenue data
findings.reasoning: Section 7.3 grants Dova audit rights against Valeant, but there is no corresponding provision granting Valeant audit rights against Dova's Net Sales calculations. Since Dova controls all the underlying sales data, shipment records, and Gross-to-Net calculations that determine Valeant's compensation, this creates fundamental information asymmetry. Valeant must rely entirely on Dova's self-reported figures without verification rights.
findings.remediation: Add reciprocal audit rights for Valeant to inspect Dova's books and records relating to Net Sales calculations, promotion fee computations, and all underlying data (Specialty Pharmacy shipments, Retail Pharmacy sales, WAC pricing, Gross-to-Net deductions) with same frequency and cost-shifting provisions.

findings.clause_text: such examination shall not cover a period of time that has previously been audited
findings.description: No re-audit rights even if new evidence of fraud or material error emerges in previously audited periods
findings.reasoning: The prohibition on re-auditing previously audited periods is absolute without exception for fraud, willful misconduct, or material errors discovered after the initial audit. If Dova's initial audit misses something due to Valeant's concealment, or if new evidence emerges later, Dova has no contractual right to re-examine that period. This creates a potential safe harbor for historical non-compliance.
findings.remediation: Add exception allowing re-audit of previously audited periods if: (a) fraud or willful misconduct is discovered; (b) material error is identified through other means; or (c) required by Government Authority inquiry.

findings.clause_text: Dova shall bear the out-of-pocket costs and expenses incurred by the Parties in connection with any such inspection or audit, unless the audit shows an undisputed over-payment for that audited period in excess of [***] of the amounts properly determined, in which case, Valeant shall reimburse Dova for its audit fees and reasonable out-of-pocket expenses
findings.description: Redacted error threshold and undefined cost allocation creates uncertainty in audit enforcement
findings.reasoning: The threshold for cost-shifting to Valeant is redacted as [***], and the clause states Dova bears costs 'incurred by the Parties' without clarifying if this means Dova bears Valeant's cooperation costs or only its own audit fees. The redacted percentage could be set so high (e.g., 10-20%) that meaningful errors below that threshold still leave Dova bearing all costs, potentially discouraging audits. Conversely, if too low, Valeant faces disproportionate risk.
findings.remediation: Specify the error threshold (recommend 5% as industry standard), clarify that 'out-of-pocket costs and expenses' means Dova's audit fees only (not Valeant's internal cooperation costs), and add that Valeant's reimbursement obligation is capped at the amount of the overpayment identified.

findings.clause_text: Any undisputed adjustments required as a result of overreporting the aggregate actual number of Details for the Product made by the Sales Representatives for a Calendar Quarter or the Quarterly Average Sales Force Size identified through the exercise of audit rights shall be made by payment by Valeant to Dova within [***] after identification of such adjustment
findings.description: Payment deadline for audit adjustments is redacted and only covers Valeant overreporting, not underreporting by Dova
findings.reasoning: The repayment deadline is redacted as [***], creating uncertainty. More critically, the adjustment mechanism only addresses 'overreporting' by Valeant (favoring Dova) with no corresponding provision for underreporting by Valeant that would require Dova to pay additional promotion fees. This is structurally one-sided. Additionally, the audit scope in 7.3 is limited to 'Valeant Activities' (Details, Sales Force Size) rather than Dova's Net Sales calculations, so this provision effectively only creates payment obligations from Valeant to Dova.
findings.remediation: Add reciprocal adjustment mechanism for underreported Details or Sales Force Size requiring Dova to pay additional promotion fees to Valeant; specify concrete payment deadline (e.g., 30 days); expand audit scope to include Dova's Net Sales calculations with corresponding adjustment rights for Valeant.

findings.clause_text: upon execution of a confidentiality agreement reasonably satisfactory to Valeant in form and substance
findings.description: Valeant retains veto power over auditor confidentiality agreement creating potential delay tactic
findings.reasoning: While this provision protects Valeant's legitimate confidentiality interests, the 'reasonably satisfactory' standard gives Valeant discretion to delay or obstruct audits by rejecting proposed confidentiality agreements. This could be used tactically to defer unfavorable audits, though the 'reasonable' qualifier provides some limitation.
findings.remediation: Specify maximum timeframe (e.g., 10 business days) for Valeant to approve or propose revisions to confidentiality agreement, with deemed approval if no response, or attach a form confidentiality agreement as Exhibit to eliminate negotiation friction.

findings.clause_text: Dova shall have the right to conduct additional 'for cause' audits to the extent necessary to address significant compliance problems relating to Valeant's obligations hereunder or in response to any inquiry, inspection, investigation or other requirements of a Government Authority in the Territory relating to the Valeant Activities
findings.description: Broad 'for cause' and government response audit rights without definition of 'significant' or cost allocation
findings.reasoning: Dova can conduct unlimited additional audits for undefined 'significant compliance problems' or government inquiries without: (a) defining what constitutes 'significant'; (b) requiring prior notice or opportunity to cure; (c) specifying who bears costs of government-mandated audits. This creates exposure for Valeant to repeated disruptive audits, particularly in a heavily regulated industry where government inquiries are common.
findings.remediation: Define 'significant compliance problems' (e.g., material breach of promotional guidelines, not minor administrative issues); add notice and cure period before for-cause audit; specify that government-mandated audit costs are borne by requesting party or as directed by Government Authority; limit frequency of for-cause audits to no more than [X] per year absent fraud finding.

findings.clause_text: referenced promotion fee calculation methodology - need to verify if Valeant has any input or verification rights
findings.description: Missing verification and audit rights for promoter in fee calculation methodology
findings.reasoning: As the promoter (Valeant), the fee calculation methodology directly impacts revenue recognition and payment accuracy. The absence of explicit input rights, verification mechanisms, or audit rights creates significant financial exposure. Without these protections, DOVA could unilaterally determine calculation methods, manipulate metrics, or resist scrutiny of reported sales data used to compute promotion fees. This is particularly acute in co-promotion structures where fee calculations typically depend on shared sales data, net sales definitions, and allocation methodologies that require mutual transparency.
findings.remediation: Negotiate for: (1) joint approval rights over the calculation methodology with specific formulas and definitions; (2) monthly/quarterly right to review underlying sales data and calculations; (3) annual audit right with 30-60 day notice and reasonable access to DOVA's records; (4) dispute resolution mechanism with escrow of disputed amounts; (5) most favored promoter clause ensuring Valeant receives terms no less favorable than any other promoter. If methodology is already fixed, demand at minimum a 'true-up' adjustment mechanism and right to independent audit.

findings.description: Material documentation gap: Section 6.2 addressing 'other payment terms' is entirely empty, creating undefined financial obligations and unlimited cost exposure in a high-value pharmaceutical co-promotion arrangement.
findings.reasoning: In co-promotion agreements, 'other payment terms' typically govern cost-sharing for joint marketing initiatives, milestone payments, pass-through expenses, promotional spend caps, and true-up mechanisms. The absence of these provisions exposes Valeant (as promoter) to: (1) unilateral cost allocation by Dova for undefined 'other' expenses; (2) unlimited marketing spend obligations without caps or approval rights; (3) ambiguity regarding whether expenses fall under base compensation (Section 6.1) or additional 'other' payments, creating double-payment risk; (4) inability to forecast or budget for compliance; and (5) litigation exposure over interpretation of implied payment obligations. This is particularly acute given Valeant's role as promoter, which typically incurs significant field force and marketing costs.
findings.remediation: Immediate negotiation required to populate Section 6.2 with: (1) Exhaustive definition of 'Other Payments' limited to specific, mutually agreed categories (e.g., 'costs of Joint Promotional Programs as defined in Section X and approved in writing by both Parties'); (2) Hard annual caps on Valeant's contribution to Other Payments (suggest: not to exceed the lesser of [X]% of Net Sales or $[Y]); (3) Prior written approval rights for Valeant for any single Other Payment exceeding $[Z] or any aggregate increase beyond forecasted amounts; (4) Explicit exclusion of indirect costs, overhead, administrative expenses, and internal field force costs from 'Other Payments' (these should be Valeant's responsibility under base terms); (5) Anti-double-dipping language clarifying that expenses reimbursable under Section 6.1 (if applicable) cannot be claimed as Other Payments under 6.2; (6) If no Other Payments are intended, protective language: 'Notwithstanding any other provision, Promoter shall have no obligation to make any payments other than those expressly set forth in Section [6.1]. For clarity, Owner shall be solely responsible for all costs and expenses not expressly allocated to Promoter in this Agreement.'

findings.clause_text: [No text provided - placeholder reference indicating 'other audit provisions' with note to check if Valeant has audit rights elsewhere]
findings.description: Missing or insufficient audit rights for Promoter (Valeant) to verify Owner's (Dova) Net Sales calculations and sales reporting
findings.reasoning: In a co-promotion agreement, Valeant (as Promoter) relies on Dova's (as Owner) sales reports to calculate revenue shares, royalties, or profit splits. If Sections 7.1 and 7.2 provide audit rights only to Dova (to verify Valeant's promotional expenses) without granting Valeant reciprocal rights to audit Dova's sales records, Valeant cannot verify the accuracy of Net Sales calculations. This creates significant financial exposure to underreporting by Dova. The contextual note suggests uncertainty about whether Valeant has any audit rights, indicating a potential one-sided provision favoring the Owner.
findings.remediation: Ensure Sections 7.1 and 7.2 (or related audit provisions) explicitly grant Valeant reciprocal audit rights: (1) Right to audit Dova's books and records relating to Net Sales of the Product; (2) No more than [once per calendar year] unless a prior audit revealed a [5%+] discrepancy; (3) [30-60 days] advance written notice; (4) Cost borne by Valeant unless discrepancy exceeds [5%] of amounts owed, in which case Dova bears costs; (5) Conducted during normal business hours with minimal disruption; (6) Limitation period of [24-36 months] post-reporting period.

findings.clause_text: responsibility for handling all safety related activities related to Product as set forth in ARTICLE 5 (including submitting all safety reports and interacting with Governmental Authorities with respect thereto) and initiating and managing any Product recalls.
findings.description: Valeant assumes primary responsibility for pharmacovigilance, safety reporting, and product recalls despite being the promoter/co-promoter rather than the marketing authorization holder.
findings.reasoning: In pharmaceutical co-promotion agreements, the owner (Dova) typically retains safety/regulatory obligations as the holder of the NDA/MA. Shifting these obligations to Valeant creates significant regulatory liability exposure, potential criminal liability for safety reporting failures, and reputational risk. Valeant may lack access to manufacturing data, batch records, or CMC information necessary to manage recalls or respond to regulatory inquiries.
findings.remediation: Negotiate for Dova to retain primary responsibility for safety reporting, regulatory interactions, and recalls, with Valeant responsible only for reporting adverse events observed during promotion and cooperating with Dova's safety efforts. If Valeant must retain these obligations, require comprehensive indemnification from Dova for any liabilities arising from product defects, manufacturing issues, or inherent safety profiles of the Product.

findings.clause_text: Valeant shall not acquire any license or other intellectual property interest, by implication or otherwise, in any technology, Know-How or other intellectual property owned or controlled by Dova or any of its Affiliates, and Dova is not providing any such technology, Know-How or other intellectual property, or any assistance related thereto, to Valeant for any use other than for the mutual benefit of the Parties as expressly contemplated hereby.
findings.description: Broad disclaimer of any implied license to Dova's background intellectual property beyond the express scope of the agreement.
findings.reasoning: While standard to prevent implied license arguments, this absolute disclaimer creates operational risk if Valeant requires access to background Know-How to effectively promote the Product (e.g., answering healthcare provider questions about formulation, mechanism of action details, or comparators). The restriction to 'mutual benefit' is vague and could limit Valeant's use of necessary technical information.
findings.remediation: Add explicit carve-out granting Valeant a limited, non-exclusive license to use Dova's background IP and Know-How strictly necessary for the performance of Valeant Activities under the agreement, limited to the Term and Territory, and solely for the purpose of promoting the Product.

findings.clause_text: if the Agreement is terminated by Dova pursuant to [***], then any Tail Period shall be immediately terminated if either Valeant or any of its Affiliates, directly or indirectly, [***] in the Territory other than the Product during such Tail Period
findings.description: Valeant's entitlement to tail period compensation or benefits is forfeited if Valeant or its affiliates engage in competitive activities during the tail period.
findings.reasoning: This creates a restrictive covenant that penalizes Valeant for exercising ordinary business rights post-termination. The mechanism effectively forces Valeant to choose between tail period revenue and the ability to market competing products. Given the redacted scope of prohibited activities [***], this could inadvertently capture Valeant's entire therapeutic portfolio or pipeline, creating a chilling effect on business operations even after contract termination.
findings.remediation: Narrow the definition of prohibited competition to only identical or bioequivalent products treating the same indication; ensure tail period termination applies only to material breaches of the non-compete, not incidental competitive activities; negotiate reciprocal restrictions on Dova regarding Valeant's confidential information and other products.

findings.clause_text: if Dova reasonably objects to the manner in which any such Dova Trademarks and Copyrights are being used, Valeant shall cease the use of any such Dova Trademarks and Copyrights in such manner upon written notice from Dova thereof
findings.description: Dova retains unilateral authority to force immediate cessation of trademark use based on subjective 'reasonable objection' without a cure period or objective standards.
findings.reasoning: This provision allows Dova to disrupt Valeant's marketing campaigns without recourse. 'Reasonable objection' is inherently subjective and could be weaponized to control commercial strategy or force compliance with Dova's marketing preferences rather than genuine trademark quality concerns. The lack of a cure period or dispute resolution mechanism before cessation is required creates immediate operational disruption risk.
findings.remediation: Modify to require Dova to specify the basis for objection in writing and provide Valeant with a 30-day cure period; limit objections to (i) non-compliance with applicable law, (ii) actual trademark dilution/tarnishment, or (iii) breach of quality standards; require good faith consultation before any cessation order becomes effective.

findings.clause_text: In the event of any disagreement between the Parties regarding any feedback received from Valeant with respect to the Product Materials, Dova shall have the right to conclusively determine such matter.
findings.description: Dova possesses absolute, final authority to determine the content of promotional materials, creating regulatory liability exposure for Valeant who must use compliant materials but lacks control over ensuring compliance.
findings.reasoning: Valeant is obligated to use only Dova-approved materials and faces direct regulatory liability (FDA warning letters, OIG actions, state AG enforcement) for off-label promotion or false advertising. However, Dova can conclusively override Valeant's compliance-related feedback. If Dova insists on non-compliant content, Valeant faces an impossible choice: use non-compliant materials (violate law) or refuse to use materials (breach agreement). This is particularly dangerous given Valeant's own regulatory history and compliance obligations.
findings.remediation: Add a compliance exception: Dora's determination shall not override Valeant's right to refuse to use materials that Valeant reasonably believes violate Applicable Law, Regulatory Approval, or Product Labeling. If a compliance dispute arises, require submission to independent regulatory counsel for determination, with costs borne by the party whose position is rejected.

findings.clause_text: In the event that Dova incurs costs and expenses for which Valeant is responsible under this Section 4.4.1, Dova may deduct such amounts from the payments due under Section 6.3 and shall include a description thereof in the applicable report under Section 6.3.
findings.description: Unilateral set-off rights allowing Dova to deduct disputed costs from payments owed to Valeant without prior dispute resolution or notice period.
findings.reasoning: This creates cash flow disruption and allows Dova to unilaterally determine disputed amounts. Valeant has no opportunity to contest the validity or amount of the deduction before it affects payments. The 'description in the report' is insufficient protection as the deduction occurs simultaneously with or before the description is provided.
findings.remediation: Require Dova to provide 30-day advance written notice of intent to deduct, allowing Valeant time to dispute the amount. If disputed, the undisputed portion may be deducted while the disputed amount is held in escrow or paid into a joint account pending resolution through the dispute resolution mechanism.

findings.clause_text: Valeant will certify in writing to Dova that all Field Force Personnel have completed the training described in this Section 4.4.1(b).
findings.description: Strict written certification requirement creates a contractual representation and potential trigger for indemnification or termination if any personnel training is incomplete.
findings.reasoning: This functions as an absolute warranty. If Valeant certifies compliance and later discovers one employee missed training (e.g., new hire, administrative error, system failure), Valeant is in immediate breach. This could trigger indemnification obligations, termination for cause, or reputational damage with Dova even for minor, correctable oversights.
findings.remediation: Modify to certify that Valeant has established training programs and requires completion before detailing, qualified with 'to the best of Valeant's knowledge' and an obligation to promptly cure any gaps discovered post-certification. Alternatively, limit certification to specific training events under Valeant's direct control.

findings.clause_text: Dova shall be solely responsible for ensuring that the Product Materials prepared and approved by it are in compliance with the Regulatory Approval for the Product, the Product Labeling and Applicable Law.
findings.description: While Dova accepts responsibility for content compliance, there is no explicit indemnification of Valeant for third-party claims or regulatory actions arising from non-compliant materials created by Dova.
findings.reasoning: Regulatory agencies and private litigants may hold Valeant jointly or severally liable for promotional materials used by its sales force, even if created by Dova. The acknowledgment of Dova's responsibility does not provide Valeant with contractual recourse for fines, penalties, or defense costs if Dova's materials violate the FDCA, FDA regulations, or state consumer protection laws. This creates a significant liability gap.
findings.remediation: Add explicit indemnification provision: Dova shall indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Valeant from any losses, fines, penalties, or defense costs arising from Product Materials' non-compliance with Applicable Law, Regulatory Approval, or Product Labeling, provided Valeant used such materials unmodified and in accordance with Dova's instructions.

findings.clause_text: Safety reporting and pharmacovigilance obligations referenced in section 2.2.6
findings.description: Critical pharmacovigilance obligations governing adverse event reporting, regulatory compliance, and potential criminal liability are incorporated by reference without the underlying Article 5 text being provided for legal review, creating unquantifiable regulatory and indemnification exposure for the Promoter.
findings.reasoning: In co-promotion agreements, the Promoter (Valeant) is typically responsible for field-level adverse event (AE) detection and initial reporting to the Owner (Dova) within strict FDA-mandated timeframes (24 hours for serious AEs). Without reviewing Article 5, it is impossible to assess: (1) whether liability for regulatory fines, Warning Letters, or consent decrees is capped or mutual; (2) if Valeant must indemnify Dova for inherent product safety risks (which should be Owner's responsibility as MAH); (3) whether Valeant's field force is subject to unacceptable strict liability for reporting delays; or (4) if patient data sharing for safety follow-up violates HIPAA/GDPR. This material omission prevents risk assessment of potential criminal and civil penalties exceeding tens of millions of dollars.
findings.remediation: 1. Obtain and review the complete text of Article 5 immediately. 2. Ensure Article 5 designates Dova as the sole Marketing Authorization Holder (MAH) responsible for regulatory submissions and master PV files. 3. Negotiate mirror indemnification: Dova indemnifies Valeant for product-related safety issues (inherent risks), while Valeant indemnifies only for its own reporting negligence or failure to forward AEs within agreed timeframes. 4. Include an aggregate liability cap applicable to regulatory fines (excluding only willful misconduct or fraud). 5. Ensure AE reporting timeframes are operationally feasible (e.g., 'next business day' for initial notification rather than strict 24-hour clock). 6. Attach a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) or Data Protection Addendum governing patient PHI exchange for safety purposes.

findings.clause_text: Payment terms and reporting referenced for set-off rights in section 4.4.1
findings.description: Unspecified set-off rights create unilateral financial exposure for promoter without procedural safeguards or limitations
findings.reasoning: Section 6.3 links payment terms to set-off rights in Section 4.4.1, but the cross-reference suggests the owner may unilaterally offset amounts owed to the promoter against unrelated claims or disputes. Without visible limitations (undisputed amounts only, prior notice, good faith dispute exclusions), this creates significant cash flow risk, accounting complexity, and enforcement difficulty for the promoter. The lack of mutuality (promoter likely cannot set off against owner) further imbalances the commercial relationship.
findings.remediation: 1. Obtain and review Section 4.4.1 immediately. 2. Negotiate express limitations: set-off permitted only for undisputed, due and payable amounts; require 30 days prior written notice; exclude amounts subject to good faith dispute; require prompt reconciliation. 3. Seek reciprocal set-off rights for promoter. 4. Carve out specific payment types (e.g., pass-through costs, reimbursable expenses) from set-off. 5. Consider requiring escrow or separate accounting if set-off rights are retained.

findings.clause_text: [Content not provided]
findings.description: License grant section content not provided for analysis, preventing assessment of IP rights scope and restrictions
findings.reasoning: Section 2.1 contains the license grants defining the scope of permitted IP use, field of use, territory, exclusivity, and sublicensing rights. In a co-promotion agreement where Valeant acts as promoter, the absence of this text prevents evaluation of whether the license is exclusive or non-exclusive, limited to specific indications, revocable, or contains onerous restrictions. This creates unquantifiable exposure regarding infringement risks, breach of restricted activities, and unclear territorial limitations.
findings.remediation: Obtain and provide the complete text of Section 2.1 including all subsections defining grant of rights, field of use, territory, exclusivity terms, and any reservations or restrictions.

findings.clause_text: Valeant shall immediately cease all Valeant Activities with respect to the Product
findings.description: No wind-down period for cessation of promotional activities creates regulatory and patient safety risks
findings.reasoning: Immediate cessation without a transition period violates standard pharmaceutical industry practice for co-promotion agreements. Valeant may have ongoing pharmacovigilance obligations, adverse event reporting requirements, and patient safety communications that cannot be terminated immediately under FDA regulations. Abrupt cessation could also disrupt ongoing clinical trials, healthcare provider relationships, and patient care continuity, exposing Valeant to regulatory enforcement and liability.
findings.remediation: Replace 'immediately' with 'within [30/60/90] days following termination' or 'as soon as reasonably practicable but in no event later than [X] days.' Add explicit carve-outs for: (a) pharmacovigilance and adverse event reporting obligations; (b) regulatory compliance activities required by FDA or other health authorities; (c) patient safety communications; and (d) transition of ongoing clinical trials or studies.

findings.clause_text: Valeant, at Dova's direction, shall immediately return to Dova or destroy in accordance with all Applicable Laws all Product Materials, reports and other tangible items provided by or on behalf of Dova to Valeant or otherwise developed or obtained by Valeant pursuant to the terms of this Agreement (other than Valeant Property)
findings.description: Dova has unilateral discretion to require destruction of materials, potentially including Valeant's proprietary derivative works and business intelligence
findings.reasoning: The phrase 'at Dova's direction' grants Dova sole discretion to choose between return and destruction. Dova could strategically require destruction of materials that include Valeant's proprietary analyses, customer insights, or derivative works to prevent Valeant from using such intelligence in future competing endeavors. The 'otherwise developed or obtained' language is overbroad and likely captures Valeant's internal business analyses, promotional strategies, and improvements to Valeant's own systems, not merely Dova's confidential information.
findings.remediation: Change to 'at Valeant's election, return or destroy' or require mutual written agreement. Narrow the scope to 'provided by Dova' only, excluding materials 'developed by Valeant using Valeant's own resources.' Explicitly exclude 'Valeant's proprietary analyses, derivative works, and business intelligence, provided that any Dova confidential information contained therein is redacted or protected in accordance with Section [X].' If Dova insists on destruction rights, require compensation for the value of destroyed proprietary materials.

findings.clause_text: each of Dova and Valeant shall, at the other Party's direction, either return to such other Party or destroy all Confidential Information of such other Party
findings.description: Generic confidential information destruction clause lacks specific data protection safeguards for patient data and personal information
findings.reasoning: In a pharmaceutical co-promotion, 'Confidential Information' necessarily includes personal data, patient health information (PHI) subject to HIPAA, and healthcare provider data. The clause does not specify destruction standards (e.g., NIST SP 800-88), data subject rights procedures (GDPR Article 17), or Business Associate Agreement (BAA) compliance requirements for PHI. This creates regulatory non-compliance risk with HIPAA, GDPR, and other privacy laws, and potential liability for inadequate data sanitization.
findings.remediation: Add specific language: 'Destruction of any personal data, patient health information, or personally identifiable information shall comply with (a) NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 1 (or successor) standards for secure data sanitization, (b) all applicable Business Associate Agreements under HIPAA, and (c) GDPR Article 28 requirements for data deletion and certification. Each Party shall provide written certification of destruction compliant with these standards within 30 days of destruction.'

findings.clause_text: accessible only to its legal or IT personnel
findings.description: Overly restrictive access to retained archival copies prevents regulatory and medical affairs personnel from fulfilling post-termination obligations
findings.reasoning: Limiting access to 'legal or IT personnel' only prevents Valeant's regulatory affairs, quality assurance, pharmacovigilance, and medical affairs staff from accessing necessary records for FDA inspections, adverse event investigations, or regulatory submissions that may be required post-termination. This creates compliance gaps with FDA record-keeping requirements (21 CFR Part 11, 21 CFR 314.81) and could prevent Valeant from defending against product liability claims or regulatory inquiries.
findings.remediation: Expand access to 'legal, IT, regulatory affairs, quality assurance, pharmacovigilance, medical affairs, and other personnel with a legitimate business need for regulatory compliance, legal defense, professional standards obligations, or audit/inspection responses.'

findings.clause_text: subject to any survival as set forth in Sections 12.5 and 12.6
findings.description: Cross-reference to undefined survival sections creates uncertainty regarding ongoing post-termination obligations
findings.reasoning: The clause references Sections 12.5 and 12.6 for survival provisions, but these sections are not provided in the analysis. Without knowing which provisions survive termination (e.g., indemnification, payment obligations, IP ownership, non-compete, confidentiality duration), Valeant cannot assess its ongoing liability exposure, insurance requirements, or contractual obligations post-termination. This creates legal uncertainty and potential for surprise liabilities.
findings.remediation: Either (a) obtain and review Sections 12.5 and 12.6 before execution, or (b) amend Section 12.4 to explicitly list all surviving obligations (e.g., 'Surviving obligations include: payment obligations accrued prior to termination, indemnification obligations, confidentiality obligations for [X] years, and IP ownership provisions').

findings.clause_text: at the request of Dova, Valeant shall certify destruction of such materials
findings.description: Administrative burden and potential liability for formal certification of destruction
findings.reasoning: The requirement to provide formal certification of destruction upon Dova's request creates administrative burden and potential contractual liability if the certification is later disputed or if residual data exists in standard IT backup systems that are not reasonably accessible. The grammatical error 'does not to return' also creates ambiguity about when the certification obligation triggers.
findings.remediation: Limit certification to written confirmation (not formal affidavit) unless required by applicable law. Correct the grammatical error to 'does not return.' Clarify that certification is not required for archival copies retained per the exception or for standard IT backup systems not reasonably accessible.

findings.clause_text: where the delivery or destruction of such files would cause undue hardship to the receiving Party
findings.description: Vague 'undue hardship' standard for retaining electronic backup files
findings.reasoning: The 'undue hardship' standard for determining when electronic backup files may be retained is subjective and likely to lead to disputes. Dova may argue that standard backup retention does not constitute 'undue hardship' to delete, while Valeant may need such backups for disaster recovery or regulatory purposes. The lack of an objective standard creates litigation risk.
findings.remediation: Replace 'undue hardship' with objective criteria such as 'technically infeasible to remove without disproportionate cost and effort' or 'resides on automated backup systems maintained in the ordinary course of business where removal would require extraordinary measures.'

findings.description: Survival provisions section is empty or omitted, creating critical uncertainty regarding post-termination obligations, duration of survival, and scope of persistent liabilities.
findings.reasoning: In a co-promotion agreement, survival provisions are essential to govern ongoing obligations after termination, including: (1) IP ownership and license rights; (2) payment obligations for products sold during the term but paid post-termination; (3) indemnification for claims arising during the term; (4) regulatory reporting obligations; and (5) confidentiality of trade secrets and patient data. Without explicit survival language, these obligations may be subject to conflicting interpretations, potentially resulting in: (a) indefinite survival of broad liabilities contrary to statute of frauds or corporate wind-down requirements; (b) premature expiration of critical protections like indemnification before statutes of limitations expire; or (c) disputes over whether revenue-sharing obligations survive for products in the distribution channel at termination.
findings.remediation: Negotiate comprehensive survival provisions that explicitly specify: (1) A enumerated list of surviving obligations (e.g., Articles X [Indemnification], Y [Confidentiality], Z [IP Ownership], Section A [Payment for Products Sold During Term]); (2) Specific survival periods tied to applicable statutes of limitations or commercially reasonable periods (e.g., indemnification survives until expiration of statute of limitations plus [X] years; confidentiality survives for [5] years or until public domain; IP ownership survives perpetually); (3) Clear commencement triggers (e.g., 'survive expiration or earlier termination of this Agreement'); (4) Explicit carve-outs for obligations that do NOT survive to avoid ambiguity; and (5) Cross-references to ensure consistency with termination payments and transition assistance obligations.

findings.clause_text: [SECTION EMPTY - No definition provided for 'Product Materials' despite governing return/destruction obligations]
findings.description: The agreement lacks any definition for 'Product Materials' in the context of post-termination return/destruction obligations, creating unlimited scope exposure for the Promoter.
findings.reasoning: As Promoter, Valeant will possess diverse materials (marketing collateral, clinical data, sales force training materials, CRM data, samples, derivative works). Without definitional boundaries, Dova can post-termination assert that virtually any materials touching the Product must be returned or destroyed. This exposes Valeant to: (1) claims for failing to return materials never intended to be covered (e.g., Valeant's proprietary sales methodologies, data analytics, or materials used across multiple products); (2) forced destruction of valuable Promoter-created derivative works that could be repurposed for non-competing products; (3) regulatory non-compliance if destruction conflicts with record-keeping laws; and (4) inability to comply with 'destruction' of digital materials while maintaining system backups. The ambiguity heavily favors the Owner (Dova) and creates immediate breach risk upon termination.
findings.remediation: Negotiate a comprehensive definition explicitly EXCLUDING: (i) materials developed independently by Promoter or pre-existing Promoter IP; (ii) general marketing concepts, methodologies, or 'know-how' used by Promoter; (iii) aggregated/anonymized data where Product-specific identifiers are removed; (iv) materials in Promoter's standard libraries or used for other products/clients; (v) materials required for regulatory compliance, legal holds, or audit defense; (vi) copies maintained in disaster recovery/archives not readily accessible. Include specific carve-out: 'Product Materials shall not include any materials created by Promoter using its own proprietary tools or methodologies, even if referencing the Product.'

findings.clause_text: [SECTION EMPTY - No format specification for tangible vs. intangible materials]
findings.description: Absence of distinction between physical materials and digital/intangible assets, creating impossible compliance obligations for electronic data.
findings.reasoning: Modern co-promotion involves digital assets (email campaigns, electronic detail aids, CRM databases, cloud-stored documents). Without specifying format, Valeant faces ambiguous obligations regarding: (1) 'Returning' digital files that inherently leave copies in system caches, server backups, and email archives; (2) Destroying data stored in enterprise systems shared across multiple products; (3) Distinguishing between Product-specific CRM data and Promoter's underlying CRM infrastructure. This creates an impossible compliance standard where Valeant cannot technically 'return' digital assets without retaining copies, yet risks claims of incomplete destruction. Additionally, cloud computing models may involve third-party sub-processors where Valeant lacks technical ability to destroy specific data subsets.
findings.remediation: Add subsection distinguishing: (a) 'Tangible Product Materials' (physical samples, printed materials, hardware) subject to return or physical destruction with certificate; (b) 'Digital Product Materials' subject to deletion from active systems only, with explicit carve-outs for: (i) archived backup tapes rotated in ordinary course; (ii) system logs/audit trails required for security; (iii) de minimis copies in system caches or temporary files; (iv) aggregated statistical data stripped of Product-specific identifiers; (v) materials on Promoter systems used for multiple clients where segregation is commercially impracticable.

findings.clause_text: [SECTION EMPTY - No temporal or territorial limitations]
findings.description: Missing temporal scope (creation date) and territorial scope limitations may sweep pre-existing materials or non-territory materials into return/destruction obligations.
findings.reasoning: Without temporal qualifiers, Dova could claim that materials created by Valeant before the agreement term but used during the term, or materials created for other territories outside the co-promotion scope, constitute 'Product Materials.' This exposes Valeant to: (1) Surrender of pre-existing trade secrets or marketing approaches adapted for the Product; (2) Destruction of materials used in non-promoted territories where Valeant has independent rights; (3) Conflicts where Valeant promotes similar products in non-conflicting territories using the same materials. The Promoter's ability to leverage existing infrastructure and cross-territory efficiencies is imperiled.
findings.remediation: Add limiting qualifiers: 'Product Materials' means only those materials: (i) created, developed, or acquired by Promoter specifically for use in the performance of this Agreement during the Term; (ii) relating solely to the Product and the Territory defined herein; (iii) excluding any materials used by Promoter for other products, clients, or in other territories; and (iv) excluding any derivative works created by Promoter using its pre-existing IP.

findings.clause_text: (iii) governing consumer
findings.description: Definition of Applicable Laws is incomplete, cutting off mid-sentence regarding consumer protection laws
findings.reasoning: The definition abruptly ends at 'governing consumer' without specifying which consumer protection laws or standards apply. This creates legal uncertainty regarding compliance obligations, particularly for the promoter who faces direct regulatory exposure in promotion activities. The incomplete definition could lead to disputes over whether specific consumer protection statutes are included or excluded.
findings.remediation: Obtain the complete text of Section 1 to verify the full scope of consumer protection laws included. Negotiate to add 'and other applicable laws' or specific statutory references to ensure clarity while avoiding unintended expansion of obligations.

findings.clause_text: as well as any state laws and regulations (i) impacting the promotion of pharmaceutical products, (ii) governing the provision of meals and other gifts to medical professionals, including pharmacists, or (iii) governing consumer
findings.description: Overly broad inclusion of all state laws without territorial limitation creates compliance burden in all 50 states
findings.reasoning: As the promoter, Valeant is obligated to comply with state laws of any jurisdiction, not just those where promotion occurs. This could impose compliance obligations under laws of states where Valeant has no promotional activities, creating unnecessary regulatory exposure and compliance costs. The clause does not limit state law applicability to the 'Territory' as defined elsewhere in the agreement.
findings.remediation: Add territorial limitation: 'state laws and regulations of the Territory' or 'states in which the Parties are performing promotion activities under this Agreement.' Alternatively, add 'to the extent applicable to the promotion activities conducted by the Parties under this Agreement.'

findings.clause_text: in the event Valeant receives safety information regarding the Product, or information regarding any safety-related regulatory request or inquiry, Valeant shall notify Dova as soon as practicable
findings.description: Overly broad and ambiguous definition of reportable 'safety information' creates strict liability exposure for promoter
findings.reasoning: The term 'safety information' is undefined and could encompass rumors, publicly available data, third-party reports, or casual mentions by healthcare providers. As promoter with extensive sales forces, Valeant is exposed to 'deemed knowledge' risks where any employee's awareness triggers reporting obligations. 'Any safety-related regulatory request or inquiry' could include general industry inquiries not specific to the Product. This creates unlimited regulatory exposure for failure to report information Valeant may not recognize as reportable.
findings.remediation: Define 'safety information' as 'credible evidence of an Adverse Event, lack of efficacy, or safety signal received by Valeant's pharmacovigilance department or designated safety officers.' Limit reporting to information specifically naming the Product. Add 'reasonable belief' standard: 'which Valeant reasonably believes constitutes safety information.' Exclude publicly available information unless specifically requested by regulators.

findings.clause_text: Valeant shall notify Dova as soon as practicable, but, in any event, within the timelines set forth in the Pharmacovigilance Agreement
findings.description: Strict notification timelines with undefined standards and no liability cap or force majeure protection
findings.reasoning: Valeant assumes absolute obligation to meet timelines in a separate agreement not yet negotiated. No cross-reference to liability caps or indemnification sections suggests unlimited liability for failure to meet reporting deadlines, which could trigger regulatory violations and contractual damages. No force majeure or excusable delay provision for technical failures or circumstances beyond Valeant's control. The 'as soon as practicable' standard is subjective and creates uncertainty.
findings.remediation: Add cross-reference: 'subject to the liability limitations set forth in Section [X].' Add force majeure carve-out for delays due to technical failures, natural disasters, or regulatory system outages. Specify that 'timelines set forth in the Pharmacovigilance Agreement' shall be 'commercially reasonable and in no event less than [24/48] hours from receipt.' Add indemnification from Dova for reporting activities performed in good faith.

findings.clause_text: Dova and Valeant (under the guidance of their respective pharmacovigilance departments, or equivalent thereof) shall identify and finalize the responsibilities the Parties shall employ... in a separate safety data exchange agreement
findings.description: Mutual obligation to negotiate Pharmacovigilance Agreement without deadlock resolution mechanism or remedy for failure to agree
findings.reasoning: The clause creates a mutual obligation to finalize a separate agreement but provides no mechanism for resolving disputes if the parties cannot agree on terms, timelines, or data exchange procedures. If negotiations deadlock, Valeant could be in breach for failing to finalize the agreement while simultaneously being unable to perform its reporting obligations without agreed procedures. No specification of fallback standards or escalation procedures.
findings.remediation: Add dispute resolution mechanism: 'In the event the Parties cannot agree on the terms of the Pharmacovigilance Agreement within [***] days, the matter shall be escalated to [senior officers/arbitration].' Alternatively, specify that 'if no agreement is reached, Valeant's obligations shall be limited to forwarding safety information to Dova within [X] days of receipt without further processing obligations.'

findings.clause_text: Dova shall be responsible for all pharmacovigilance activities regarding the Product, including signal detection, medical surveillance, risk management, medical literature review and monitoring, Adverse Event reporting and responses to Governmental Authority requests or enquiries, and shall provide information related thereto to Valeant
findings.description: Asymmetric responsibility allocation without indemnification for promoter relying on owner's pharmacovigilance activities
findings.reasoning: While Dova assumes primary pharmacovigilance responsibility, Valeant as co-promoter remains exposed to regulatory action and liability for promotion based on inadequate safety information from Dova. The clause does not require Dova to indemnify Valeant for failures in signal detection, missed adverse events, or inadequate responses to regulatory inquiries. Valeant has no audit rights over Dova's pharmacovigilance activities to verify compliance.
findings.remediation: Add indemnification: 'Dova shall indemnify Valeant for any losses arising from Dova's failure to perform pharmacovigilance activities in accordance with Applicable Laws or this Agreement.' Add audit rights: 'Valeant shall have the right to audit Dova's pharmacovigilance records upon reasonable notice to verify compliance.' Add requirement for Dova to maintain pharmacovigilance/errors and omissions insurance.

findings.clause_ref: Cross-reference to indemnification provisions to confirm protection for pharmacovigilance reporting activities
findings.clause_text: Cross-reference to indemnification provisions to confirm protection for pharmacovigilance reporting activities
findings.description: Placeholder reference without actual indemnification language—pharmacovigilance reporting lacks explicit contractual protection
findings.reasoning: Pharmacovigilance activities carry significant regulatory and liability exposure (FDA adverse event reporting, global safety obligations, potential whistleblower/False Claims Act exposure). The 'cross-reference' language suggests this is a drafting placeholder or incomplete integration. Without explicit indemnification terms: (1) promoter (Valeant) faces unallocated liability for safety reporting errors, delays, or omissions; (2) statutory adverse event reporting obligations may trigger penalties where liability is disputed; (3) successor liability risks exist if DOVA's safety data is incomplete; (4) insurance coverage gaps may emerge where indemnity is unclear. The co-promotion structure typically requires joint safety committees and defined AE routing protocols—absent explicit indemnification, Valeant assumes disproportionate exposure as the party with direct HCP/patient contact.
findings.remediation: Negotiate explicit indemnification clause: (a) DOVA indemnifies Promoter for third-party claims arising from DOVA's safety database errors, regulatory filings, or product labeling; (b) mutual indemnification for claims arising from each party's own AE reporting failures; (c) carve-out for willful misconduct/gross negligence; (d) survival period through statute of limitations plus regulatory lookback periods; (e) insurance requirement: DOVA maintains product liability coverage naming Promoter as additional insured with minimum $50M per occurrence; (f) regulatory defense cost advancement. If DOVA resists, seek liability cap at annual fees paid with floor at $10M, and require joint safety committee with veto on safety communications.

findings.clause_ref: Review of liability cap provisions to confirm coverage of pharmacovigilance breach damages
findings.description: Liability cap provisions lack explicit treatment of pharmacovigilance breach damages, creating uncertainty whether such damages are subject to or excluded from contractual liability limitations.
findings.reasoning: Pharmacovigilance breaches in pharmaceutical co-promotion agreements can result in severe regulatory penalties, patient safety liabilities, and reputational damage that far exceed standard contractual liability caps (typically limited to annual fees). The absence of specific language addressing whether pharmacovigilance-related damages are carved out from liability caps creates significant exposure for the promoter, who may face unlimited liability for regulatory fines arising from safety reporting failures, or conversely, be unable to recover full damages from the owner if the owner breaches pharmacovigilance obligations and the cap applies to limit recovery.
findings.remediation: Negotiate explicit carve-out language stating that liability caps do not apply to damages arising from pharmacovigilance breaches, regulatory violations, or failure to comply with adverse event reporting obligations. Alternatively, establish a separate, substantially higher liability sub-cap specifically for pharmacovigilance-related damages (e.g., 3-5x annual fees). Ensure indemnification provisions explicitly cover pharmacovigilance breaches by either party and that such indemnification is not subject to the general liability cap.

findings.clause_text: [TEXT NOT PROVIDED - Section title: 'Complete text of Section 1 to verify full scope of consumer protection laws referenced']
findings.description: Missing clause text prevents assessment of consumer protection law compliance obligations and creates unquantifiable regulatory exposure
findings.reasoning: In pharmaceutical co-promotion agreements, Section 1 typically contains fundamental representations, warranties, and compliance obligations regarding consumer protection laws (including FDA regulations, False Claims Act, Anti-Kickback Statute, and state consumer protection acts). Without the actual text, it is impossible to determine if these obligations are: (1) one-sided (imposed only on Promoter), (2) uncapped (creating unlimited liability for statutory violations), (3) broadly worded to include all consumer protection laws rather than only those applicable to specific promotional activities, or (4) lacking knowledge qualifiers for representations. This creates unquantifiable compliance risk, particularly given the severe penalties associated with FDA promotional guideline violations and False Claims Act liability in pharmaceutical marketing.
findings.remediation: Request complete text of Section 1 immediately before proceeding with agreement execution. Pending receipt, assume broad, one-sided compliance obligations exist and negotiate the following protections: (1) explicit limitation of liability for statutory/regulatory violations (capped at fees paid or insurance limits), (2) specific carve-out for indirect, consequential, and punitive damages arising from consumer protection claims, (3) mutual indemnification rather than unilateral Promoter indemnification for consumer protection claims, (4) knowledge and materiality qualifiers for all representations regarding compliance, (5) obligation to comply only with laws 'applicable to party's specific role and activities' rather than all consumer protection laws generally, and (6) exclusion of liability for actions taken at the direction of or with the approval of the other party.

findings.clause_text: Except to Affiliates of Valeant, Valeant's rights and obligations under this Section 2.1 are non-transferable, non-assignable, and non-delegable.
findings.description: Absolute prohibition on assignment and delegation prevents Valeant from transferring rights to successors in M&A transactions or restructuring
findings.reasoning: Standard commercial agreements typically permit assignment to successors or in connection with a change of control. This clause prevents Valeant from assigning the agreement to a purchaser in an asset sale or merger, potentially creating a material adverse change or default scenario in an M&A context. The carve-out for Affiliates is insufficient as it doesn't cover non-affiliate successors.
findings.remediation: Negotiate for the right to assign the agreement to successors in connection with a merger, acquisition, or sale of all or substantially all assets, provided the assignee assumes all obligations. Alternatively, require that Dova's consent to assignment not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed.

findings.clause_text: Valeant guarantees the performance of all actions, agreements and obligations to be performed by its Affiliates under the terms and conditions of this Agreement.
findings.description: Unlimited guarantee of all affiliate obligations creates uncapped liability exposure for Valeant without carve-outs for willful misconduct or regulatory violations
findings.reasoning: Valeant is liable for 'all actions, agreements and obligations' of its Affiliates, which could include regulatory compliance failures, data privacy breaches, or anti-kickback violations committed by Affiliates. Unlike standard guarantee provisions limited to payment obligations, this covers performance of all contractual covenants. There is no carve-out for Affiliates' willful misconduct, fraud, or independent actions outside Valeant's control.
findings.remediation: Limit the guarantee to payment obligations only, or cap the liability at a specific dollar amount or percentage of fees received. Add carve-outs for losses arising from Affiliates' willful misconduct, fraud, or violations of law committed contrary to Valeant's written policies. Alternatively, require that Valeant be given prompt notice and opportunity to cure affiliate defaults before liability attaches.

findings.clause_text: Except to Affiliates of Valeant, Valeant shall not subcontract the Valeant Activities with any Third Party (including any contract sales force).
findings.description: Prohibition on subcontracting prevents use of contract sales organizations (CSOs) and limits operational flexibility
findings.reasoning: In pharmaceutical co-promotion agreements, it is standard practice to allow the use of contract sales forces (CSOs) to flex capacity or cover geographic gaps. This absolute prohibition (except for Affiliates) forces Valeant to use only its own employees, potentially increasing costs and reducing scalability. This is particularly burdensome given that Valeant must guarantee affiliate performance but cannot use non-affiliate CSOs.
findings.remediation: Negotiate for the right to subcontract Valeant Activities to approved contract sales forces and other Third Party providers, subject to Dova's prior written consent (not to be unreasonably withheld) and compliance with Dova's reasonable training and compliance requirements. Alternatively, permit subcontracting for specific operational functions (e.g., data analytics, logistics) while retaining direct control of detailing activities.

findings.clause_text: Valeant shall have no right to, and shall not, conduct the Valeant Activities for the Product outside the Specialty or outside the Territory or for use outside the Field.
findings.description: Strict field and territory restrictions prevent Valeant from pursuing new indications or geographic expansions without amendment
findings.reasoning: If the Product receives FDA approval for new indications (outside the Field) or if the Territory is expanded, Valeant is explicitly excluded from conducting activities in those areas unless the Agreement is amended. This creates a competitive disadvantage if Dova decides to promote in these new areas alone or with a different partner. Unlike standard agreements that provide rights of first refusal or automatic inclusion for expanded indications, this is a hard exclusion.
findings.remediation: Add a right of first refusal or right to negotiate in good faith for Valeant to extend the Agreement to new indications, expanded Territory, or additional Fields on commercially reasonable terms. Alternatively, provide that if Dova engages a third party for such expanded rights, Valeant must be offered terms no less favorable.

findings.clause_text: [***] shall constitute the "Speaker Program Threshold".
findings.description: Material financial threshold defining cost-sharing obligations is redacted, preventing assessment of cost exposure
findings.reasoning: The Speaker Program Threshold determines when cost-sharing obligations trigger for excess speaker programs. Without knowing this number (e.g., whether it is 50, 100, or 500 programs), Valeant cannot model its financial obligations, budget for speaker program costs, or assess the materiality of the cost-sharing provision. This is a critical gap that prevents proper risk assessment and contract valuation.
findings.remediation: Obtain the unredacted threshold number immediately. If the threshold is unreasonably low, negotiate for a higher threshold or a specific annual cap on Valeant's contribution to speaker program costs (e.g., not to exceed $X or Y% of annual budget).

findings.clause_text: In the event that Dova incurs costs and expenses for which Valeant is responsible under this Section 3.5.2, Dova may deduct such amounts from the payments due under Section 6.3 and shall include a description thereof in the applicable report under Section 6.3.
findings.description: Unilateral set-off rights against milestone or royalty payments create cash flow uncertainty and dispute risk
findings.reasoning: Dova can unilaterally determine that Valeant owes costs under Section 3.5.2 and deduct these amounts from payments due under Section 6.3 (likely royalties or milestones) without prior dispute resolution, mutual agreement on the amount, or Valeant's consent. This creates significant cash flow risk if Dova interprets 'additional incremental costs' broadly. While Dova must include a description, there is no requirement for Valeant's prior approval of the deduction or a cure period.
findings.remediation: Require that any set-off be limited to undisputed amounts, or require prior written notice and a 30-day cure/consultation period before deduction. Alternatively, require mutual agreement on the amount owed or submission to a neutral accountant/arbitrator for disputed amounts before set-off is permitted.

findings.clause_text: Valeant shall have the right to review and approve (acting reasonably and in good faith) any such excess speaker programs, including with respect to the number of speakers approved to speak on the Product as part of the speaker programs, the rates paid to speakers at such speaker programs and the rules regarding attendees who may attend such speaker programs (including frequency of attendance).
findings.description: Operational approval rights over speaker program details create potential shared liability for Anti-Kickback Statute and Sunshine Act compliance
findings.reasoning: By exercising approval rights over speaker selection, payment rates, and attendee rules, Valeant may be deemed a 'sponsor' or 'organizer' of the speaker programs under the Anti-Kickback Statute (AKS) and Sunshine Act (Open Payments). If Dova selects a high-prescribing physician as a speaker and Valeant approves the rate, Valeant could share liability if the arrangement is deemed remuneration for referrals. The 'acting reasonably and in good faith' standard does not eliminate this regulatory exposure.
findings.remediation: Clarify that Dova retains sole responsibility for compliance with all healthcare laws (AKS, Sunshine Act, PhRMA Code) regarding speaker programs. Limit Valeant's approval rights to 'commercial reasonableness' explicitly excluding compliance responsibility, or require that all speaker programs comply with Dova's standard operating procedures which Dova warrants are compliant with applicable law.

findings.clause_text: the additional incremental costs and expenses associated with training necessary to address the number of the speaker programs above and below the Speaker Program Threshold
findings.description: Ambiguous cost allocation language could require Valeant to share training costs for all speaker programs, not just excess programs
findings.reasoning: The phrase 'above and below the Speaker Program Threshold' is ambiguous. It could be interpreted as: (1) training costs for programs both above and below the threshold (i.e., all programs), or (2) incremental training costs attributable to the increased volume of programs above the threshold (with 'and below' being a drafting error). If interpreted broadly, Valeant could be responsible for 50% of all training costs for speaker programs once the threshold is exceeded, not just the incremental costs of the excess programs.
findings.remediation: Clarify that Valeant is only responsible for incremental training costs directly attributable to speaker programs conducted in excess of the Speaker Program Threshold, and explicitly exclude training costs for programs within the threshold. Define 'incremental' as the marginal cost of training additional speakers beyond the base threshold capacity.

findings.clause_text: If the Marketing Sub-Committee unanimously agrees that such excess speaker programs should be conducted...
findings.description: Unanimous consent requirement for excess speaker programs creates deadlock risk and may prevent optimal marketing strategies
findings.reasoning: The requirement for unanimous agreement by the Marketing Sub-Committee means either party can veto excess speaker programs. While this protects Valeant from unwanted costs, it also means that if Valeant disagrees (even unreasonably), Dova can proceed but Valeant pays nothing. However, if the program is strategically important for market development but Valeant is cash-constrained or disagrees with the strategy, the unanimous requirement creates deadlock. More importantly, if Dova proceeds alone, Valeant loses the benefit of coordinated messaging.
findings.remediation: Change the standard from 'unanimously agrees' to 'does not object within [X] business days' or provide that if one party wishes to conduct excess programs and bears 100% of the cost, it may do so without unanimous consent, provided it complies with the agreement's compliance requirements.

In co-promotion agreements, institutional account management provisions (covering hospitals, GPOs, and IDNs) typically include: (1) exclusive allocation of strategic accounts to the owner (Dova), preventing promoter (Valeant) access to high-value customers; (2) unfettered discretion by Dova to direct institutional strategy while Valeant bears execution liability; (3) performance metrics for institutional accounts that trigger termination or penalty provisions; (4) broad indemnification for IP or regulatory violations arising from institutional presentations; and (5) post-termination restrictions on soliciting institutional accounts. findings.clause_text: WHEREAS, the Parties believe that it would be mutually beneficial to collaborate on promotional activities for the Product and, accordingly, Dova desires that Valeant conduct certain promotional activities, and Valeant desires to conduct such activities, for the Product in the Territory;
findings.description: Assumption of promotional liability for third-party pharmaceutical product without visible indemnification, liability caps, or regulatory compliance safeguards
findings.reasoning: As the promoter (Valeant), this recital establishes that Valeant will conduct promotional activities for Dova's Product. In pharmaceutical co-promotion, this exposes Valeant to significant liability risks including: (1) product liability claims arising from patient use of the drug, (2) regulatory enforcement actions by FDA/DOJ for off-label promotion or advertising violations (even if unintentional), (3) third-party intellectual property infringement claims related to the product itself, and (4) False Claims Act exposure. Without visible operative provisions indemnifying Valeant for product-related claims and capping liability for promotional activities, Valeant could face unlimited liability for a product it does not manufacture, control, or own. The recitals suggest Valeant 'desires' these activities, which could be used to argue assumption of risk in any dispute.
findings.remediation: Ensure operative sections (not visible in this excerpt) include: (1) Comprehensive indemnification from Dova covering all product liability, regulatory violations arising from product composition/manufacturing/labeling, and third-party IP claims; (2) Explicit exclusion of liability for product defects, efficacy, or safety; (3) Mutual liability cap limiting Valeant's exposure to fees received or a specified dollar amount (e.g., $X million or 12 months of fees); (4) Right to terminate immediately without penalty if product safety issues arise; (5) Regulatory compliance allocation specifying Dova is responsible for product labeling, manufacturing compliance, and initial regulatory approvals, while Valeant is only responsible for promotional activities in compliance with provided materials.

findings.clause_text: WHEREAS, Dova has developed and has rights to market and sell the Product (as defined below) in the Territory;
findings.description: Reliance on unqualified representations regarding Dova's product rights and development status without visible warranties or freedom-to-operate covenants
findings.reasoning: The recitals contain material representations that Dova 'has developed' the Product and 'has rights to market and sell' it in the Territory. These statements are fundamental to Valeant's decision to invest resources in promotion. If Dova does not in fact have clear title, freedom to operate (FTO) under third-party patents, or valid regulatory approvals, Valeant could expend substantial resources promoting a product that cannot be legally sold, or face infringement litigation from third parties. While recitals are often considered non-binding preamble language, they can be incorporated by reference into operative provisions or used as evidence of representations made to induce entry into the agreement. Without visible warranties, covenants, or indemnification in the operative sections backing these recital statements, Valeant bears the risk of Dova's representations being inaccurate.
findings.remediation: Ensure operative sections include explicit representations and warranties from Dova that: (a) it is the sole owner or exclusive licensee of all intellectual property rights necessary to develop, manufacture, use, and commercialize the Product; (b) the Product does not infringe, misappropriate, or violate any third-party intellectual property rights; (c) it has obtained all necessary regulatory approvals (NDA, IND, etc.) for the Product in the Territory; (d) the Product is being manufactured in compliance with cGMP; and (e) there are no pending or threatened claims challenging Dova's rights to the Product. Include survival periods for these warranties (e.g., 3-5 years post-termination) and specific indemnification for breach of these representations.

In a pharmaceutical co-promotion agreement, redacted provisions typically include the most risk-critical terms: (1) detailed promotional obligations and performance metrics (minimum spending requirements, headcount requirements, sales targets); (2) financial terms (payment schedules, cost-sharing arrangements, penalties for underperformance); (3) liability caps and indemnification scope (whether product liability is capped, whether Valeant is indemnified for regulatory actions); (4) termination rights (whether Valeant can terminate for convenience, notice periods, transition assistance obligations); (5) IP ownership of co-created promotional materials; and (6) data privacy obligations regarding patient data or prescriber data. findings.description: Incomplete counterparts clause may lack electronic signature validation and execution certainty provisions
findings.reasoning: Only the heading '13.18 Counterparts' and page number '47' are visible. While counterparts clauses are typically boilerplate, modern pharmaceutical agreements require specific language to ensure: (1) electronic signatures (DocuSign, Adobe Sign) are deemed valid and binding originals, (2) delivery of executed counterparts by email/PDF constitutes valid execution, and (3) all counterparts together constitute one agreement. Without visible language addressing electronic execution, there is a risk that electronically executed versions (which are standard in modern transactions) could be challenged as invalid, or that parties could dispute which version is controlling. Additionally, if the clause permits execution in any number of counterparts without requiring exchange, it could create uncertainty about when the agreement becomes effective.
findings.remediation: Ensure the full counterparts clause includes explicit language stating: 'This Agreement may be executed in counterparts, each of which shall be deemed an original and all of which together shall constitute one and the same instrument. Electronic signatures (including PDF, DocuSign, Adobe Sign, or similar electronic signature technology) shall be deemed original signatures for all purposes. Delivery of executed counterparts by email or other electronic transmission shall constitute valid and binding execution.' Additionally, specify that the Agreement becomes effective upon execution by both Parties, regardless of whether counterparts have been exchanged.
